title: Bayes' Theorem and the Base Rate Fallacy

paper.title: An Essay towards Solving a Problem in the Doctrine of Chances

hook: A 99% accurate test for a rare disease can still be wrong most of the time when it says you're sick. Why?

symbols.meaning: Sensitivity: probability of positive test given disease
False positive rate: probability of positive test given no disease
Posterior probability of disease given a positive test

equation.caption: Bayes' theorem for a binary test.

explorations.title: Rare disease, accurate test
explorations.predict: If the disease is rare (1 in 1000) and the test is 99% sensitive and 5% false positive, what is the chance you have the disease after a positive test?
explorations.observe: The posterior is about 1.9%. Even with a positive test, the disease is unlikely.
explorations.why: Because the disease is rare, the number of false positives from the large healthy population outweighs the true positives from the small diseased population. The denominator P(+) is dominated by the false positive term.

explorations.title: Common disease, same test
explorations.predict: If the disease is common (10% prevalence) with the same test, what is the posterior now?
explorations.why: With higher prevalence, the true positive term P(+|D)P(D) becomes larger relative to the false positive term, so the posterior increases.

limitation: Assumes the test's sensitivity and false positive rate are known exactly and do not vary between individuals or populations. In reality, these can depend on disease severity, comorbidities, and test administration.
misconception: Many people think a positive test on a 99% accurate test means a 99% chance of disease. Actually, the posterior depends heavily on prevalence.

claims.text: Bayes' theorem gives the posterior probability of disease given a positive test.
The posterior is low when prevalence is low, even with high sensitivity and low false positive rate.
The toy model assumes a fixed population of 1000 and exact probabilities.

outcomes.outcome: Calculate posterior probability using Bayes' theorem.
Explain why a rare disease leads to a low posterior even with an accurate test.
Interpret the counts of true/false positives and negatives out of 1000 people.
